source_title: Ben Affleck Makes $100K Donation to Fight Pediatric Epilepsy - People.com
source_excerpt:
The actor was honored at the 20th Anniversary Gala for The Care & Cure Institute
Vanessa Etienne is a Staff Writer for PEOPLE on the Health team. She joined the brand in 2021.
Ben Affleck spoke about his personal connection to epilepsy at The Care & Cure Institute’s 20th Anniversary Gala
The nonprofit addresses shortages of specialists who diagnose and treat children with epilepsy
The event raised nearly $2 million and has helped train doctors who cared for more than 350,000 children
Ben Affleck is lending his voice to a personal issue.
On Oct. 29, the 54-year-old actor attended the 20th Anniversary Gala for The Care & Cure Institute (C&CI) , a nonprofit that works to address the shortage of specialists who diagnose and treat epilepsy in children.
Ahead of November’s National Epilepsy Awareness Month, Affleck made a $100,000 donation during the event and was honored for his longstanding philanthropic work . He then gave a heartfelt speech about his personal connection to epilepsy.
“Epilepsy isn’t abstract to me. I’ve watched people I care about deal with it, and I’ve seen how much it matters when a family can get in front of the right doctor quickly,” he said. “Spending time at UCLA with the physicians doing this work was humbling. These are specialists who chose to dedicate their careers to kids, and the Care & Cure Institute is making sure there are more of them.”

Affleck said he was proud to see the work that Andrew Gumpert and Mark Borman, co-founders of the Care & Cure Institute, are doing.
During his speech, he also commended the other attendees who donated. The gala raised nearly $2 million.
“Tonight I’m saying thank you for giving and giving generously. You have really changed lives,” he said, vowing to continue to raise awareness and funds.
“Here’s the thing. None of us get to choose whether it’s our child or someone else’s child who gets sick. That’s the truth,” Affleck said. “But all of us get to choose what we’re going to do about the children who do get sick. Twenty years ago you couldn’t find enough doctors for your kids so you made more, and because you did, more than 350,000 children have been cared for by doctors you helped train. Let’s finish what you started.”
